topics.label: Trade and Cultural Exchange
topics.definition: Sharing ideas and practices through contact.
facts: Sea routes connected communities with visitors carrying goods and ideas. Contact could happen through several places and people.
People could share knowledge without every community becoming the same.
A single imported object does not prove what everyone believed.
quiz: Visitors bring goods and discuss ideas with a coastal community. Which explanation fits?
Trade could create chances to share goods and ideas
Trade always made all communities identical
Goods moved without any people
One meeting changed every island at once
retry: A coastal community trades but keeps some local customs. What does this show?
Contact and local differences can exist together
Trade requires all customs to disappear
Different customs prove no contact
Every visitor follows one rule
practice: What can travel with people along trade routes?
hard: A learner finds an imported bowl and says everyone followed the maker's religion. What is needed?
More evidence about belief, not only one object
Only a guess about its color
A bigger picture
A claim that all traders believed alike

topics.label: How Islam Spread Gradually
topics.definition: A religion followed by Muslims.
facts: Islam became established in parts of Sulu and Mindanao before Spanish colonization. Connections with Muslim merchants, teachers and local communities mattered.
The process was gradual and differed by place. It was not one event that changed every community.
Trade was one connection among several, not a complete explanation by itself.
quiz: A history report describes merchants, teachers and local leaders over time. What does it suggest about Islam's spread?
Several people and connections helped a gradual process
Every island changed religion on one day
Only one boat explains the whole process
Local communities had no role
retry: Two communities adopted religious practices at different times. Which idea helps explain this?
Change could be gradual and differ by place
Every community changed at the same moment
Different dates prove no contact
All local histories must be identical
practice: Islam spread gradually to some southern communities
Every Philippine island changed at once
hard: A report mentions trade but leaves out teachers and local choices. What should improve?
Include other supported roles in the process
Say goods changed beliefs by themselves
Hide local people
Treat all places as the same

topics.label: Learning Respectfully About Islam
topics.definition: A person who follows Islam.
facts: Islamic teachings include belief in one God, prayer, charitable giving and fasting during Ramadan.
Learning about a religion in history is not a request to perform its worship. Students may have different beliefs.
Respectful questions help understanding. No learner should be asked to speak for all Muslims.
quiz: A class studies Muslim communities. Which statement is accurate?
Islamic teachings include belief in one God and charitable giving
Every Muslim community has exactly the same local customs
Studying a religion means every student must follow it
Only one student can explain all Muslims
retry: A learner asks a Muslim classmate to speak for every Muslim community. What is a better approach?
Use reliable sources and recognize different experiences
Treat one answer as everyone's view
Assume all local customs are identical
Ask the classmate to perform worship for a grade
hard: A class wants an activity about religious history. Which is suitable?
Compare supported historical information respectfully
Require worship to pass
Rank classmates' religions
Make jokes about unfamiliar practices

topics.label: Growing Communities
topics.definition: People connected through relationships and shared life.
facts: Teachers, families, local leaders and maritime contacts helped Muslim communities develop. Their experiences were not all the same.
Religious learning and community relationships could continue across generations.
Changes in belief, leadership and trade were connected, but each place had its own history.
quiz: A report shows families teaching children, leaders building relationships and visitors arriving by sea. What does it explain?
Several connected roles in community development
Growth caused by goods alone
One identical history for every place
A process with no local people
retry: Two Muslim communities have different local traditions. What is a careful response?
Recognize different local histories within shared religious connections
Say one community cannot be Muslim
Assume every custom must match
Remove local voices from the account
practice: Who could help pass on community knowledge?
hard: An account lists leaders but ignores families. What question could improve it?
How did families and other members contribute?
Why do local people never matter?
Can one leader explain every person?
Should all sources be removed?

topics.label: Leadership in Sulu
topics.definition: A political community or state led by a sultan.
facts: The Sultanate of Sulu developed during the fifteenth century. It linked leadership with communities, relationships and trade.
A sultanate was not the same as every barangay. It did not govern the whole Philippine archipelago.
Different communities had different political arrangements and histories.
quiz: A learner says the Sultanate of Sulu ruled every Philippine island. What is the careful correction?
It was important in Sulu but did not govern the whole archipelago
It had no connection to communities
Every barangay was the same sultanate
All islands had one identical government
retry: A museum caption describes a community led by a sultan. Which term fits?
Sultanate
A pottery workshop
An archipelago with one culture
A modern classroom
practice: A leader associated with a sultanate
A name for all island chiefs
hard: A report compares a barangay and the Sultanate of Sulu. What should it do?
Study their differences instead of treating them as identical
Give every leader the same role
Assume one ruled every island
Ignore differences in scale and relationships

topics.label: Waterways Connect Communities
topics.definition: A group of islands.
facts: The Philippines is an archipelago. Water separates islands but also provides routes between them.
Boats could carry people, goods and messages. Rivers could connect inland places to the coast.
A route depends on the places connected, the boat and local conditions. Not every trip followed the same path.
quiz: Two island communities want to exchange goods. What could help them cross the water?
A boat suited to the journey
A cart used only on land
A basket with no boat
A path that ignores the sea
retry: A river runs from an inland settlement to the coast. How could it help people stay connected?
Boats could move along suitable parts of the river
It makes all land travel impossible
It proves every river can carry every boat
It removes the need to plan a journey
hard: A community has both a river route and a sea crossing. What should travellers check?
Whether their boat and each part of the route suit the journey
Only the color of the boat
Whether all rivers have the same depth
Whether planning can be skipped

topics.label: The Boats of Butuan
topics.definition: A name associated with early plank-built boats found in Butuan.
facts: Boat remains found in Butuan give evidence of early boatbuilding and water travel. Archaeologists study the wood and the way parts join.
The remains help us ask how builders made strong boats. They do not preserve every journey or every person aboard.
A modern model helps explain construction, but a model is not the original ancient boat.
quiz: A museum shows old boat remains found in Butuan. What do they help us study?
Early boatbuilding and water travel
The names of every sailor
The exact weather on every voyage
The rules of every village
retry: A class sees a newly built model of a balangay. How should they describe it?
A model that helps explain an older boatbuilding tradition
The original boat recovered from the ground
Proof of every voyage made long ago
A record listing every sailor
practice: Which find best supports the study of early boats?
Old wooden boat parts from an excavated site
A plastic toy without a source
hard: A boat part has no passenger list. What should a careful learner avoid?
Inventing names of people who sailed in it
Asking how its parts joined
Comparing it with other finds
Reading the museum label

topics.label: Joining a Wooden Boat
topics.definition: The work and skills used to make boats.
facts: Butuan boats were built from wooden planks. Builders used skilled ways of joining parts, including pegs and lashings.
The shape and joints of a boat matter for its use. Building requires knowledge, suitable materials and careful work.
Different boats can be made in different ways. One boat design does not describe every Philippine watercraft.
quiz: A builder checks wooden joints before a trip. Why does this work matter?
The joined parts help the boat hold together
The wood color decides the travel time
Every boat uses exactly the same joints
Joints replace all sailing skills
retry: Two old boats have different shapes. What is a careful response?
Study how each was built and used
Assume one must be fake
Say all boats had one shape
Ignore the parts and guess
practice: What skill helps people make a wooden boat?
Knowing how suitable parts can join
hard: A model has loose planks. What should its makers do before testing it?
Check and repair the joints
Add a name and ignore the problem
Assume all joints are strong
Remove every support

topics.label: Reading Travel Conditions
topics.definition: Travelling or working at sea.
facts: Seafaring needs knowledge of water, weather, routes and the boat. People learned through experience and teaching.
Winds and currents can affect a journey. A planned route may need to change when conditions change.
Careful preparation reduces risks but cannot promise a safe trip in every situation.
quiz: A crew sees worsening weather before leaving. What is the careful choice?
Check conditions and delay or change the plan if needed
Leave because all trips must keep the same time
Ignore the boat and weather
Assume the sea never changes
retry: Travellers learn that a route is unsafe today. How can they use their knowledge?
Choose a safer plan after checking conditions
Follow the old plan without checking
Guess that every route is safe
Use boat color to predict the weather
practice: Which information helps plan a sea trip?
Only the name of the boat
hard: A familiar route has changed conditions. What does experience help a crew do?
Notice changes and reconsider the journey
Guarantee nothing can go wrong
Avoid checking the weather
Treat every day as identical

topics.label: Caring for Boat Evidence
topics.definition: The study of past life through objects and places.
facts: Archaeologists record where boat parts are found and how they relate to nearby objects. Their place in the ground can be important evidence.
Old waterlogged wood can be fragile. Trained specialists decide how to care for it.
If you find a possible old object, tell a responsible adult or museum authority. Do not dig it out or take it home.
quiz: A learner sees old-looking wood near a heritage site. What should the learner do?
Report it and leave it in place
Pull it out to keep as a prize
Scrape it to see its color
Sell it before anyone records it
retry: Why do archaeologists record where boat parts were found?
The location helps explain the find with other evidence
Location makes all other study unnecessary
It identifies every sailor by itself
It proves every object is the same age
practice: Who should decide how to preserve fragile old wood?
hard: A friend wants to remove a small part from a museum model or display. What should you do?
Stop and ask museum staff for guidance
Take it because it is small
Hide it in a bag
Assume a display needs no care

title: Trade Networks with Neighboring Asian Societies

topics.label: Many Places, Many Links
topics.definition: Connected places and people involved in exchange.
facts: Early communities in the islands had links with other Asian societies before Spanish rule. Ships and coastal routes helped goods move.
A network can include several stops and many traders. A good may pass through more than one place.
Finding an imported object does not prove a direct trip from its maker to its final owner.
quiz: A bowl made abroad reaches an island through several ports. What does this show?
Goods can move through a trade network
Every owner visited the place where it was made
Trade required only one stop everywhere
All goods were made in one village
retry: A learner finds a picture of an imported jar at a local site. Which question needs more evidence?
Did the jar travel directly from its maker to this site?
Was the jar found at the site described?
Does the label call it imported?
Is a jar shown in the picture?
practice: Places and people linked by exchange
hard: Three ports pass goods onward. What should a map show?
The links among the ports
Only the last owner and no route
A claim that all traders used one ship
A route based on a guess alone

topics.label: Ceramics as Trade Clues
topics.definition: An object made from clay and hardened by heat.
facts: Imported ceramics found in Philippine sites help show contact with other Asian places. Some were made in China and other parts of Asia.
Researchers compare shapes, materials and designs with objects whose origins are known.
One bowl cannot reveal every reason for trade. Its place, date and nearby finds also matter.
quiz: Researchers compare a bowl with ceramics from known workshops. Why?
To investigate where it may have been made
To learn every owner without other clues
To prove all bowls had one use
To make its find location unimportant
retry: A site has both local pots and imported bowls. What can the finds suggest?
Local production and outside contacts could exist together
All local skills had disappeared
Every pot was made abroad
Trade stopped people making useful things
practice: A leaf used as a wrapper
hard: A bowl has no clear find record. How should a learner respond?
Recognize that missing information limits the explanation
Invent a location
Claim its full journey is certain
Ignore the need for evidence

topics.label: Why People Exchanged Goods
topics.definition: Something people can use to meet a need.
facts: Communities had different resources and skills. Exchange could help people obtain useful or valued goods.
People also made things locally. Trading did not mean all communities stopped farming, fishing or crafting.
Goods could serve daily needs, ceremonies or social purposes. We should check evidence rather than assume one purpose.
quiz: A community makes baskets but needs goods from elsewhere. Why might it trade?
To obtain goods not easily available locally
To prove local basket-making has no value
To stop every local activity forever
To make all places have the same resources
retry: Imported jars are found alongside locally made tools. What is a careful idea?
Exchange could support life alongside local work
Every tool must also be imported
The community had no skills
Only imported goods were useful
practice: Why can different resources encourage trade?
One place may have something another needs
Every place has exactly the same products
hard: A trader offers a valued good. What should an investigator avoid assuming?
That everyone wanted it for exactly the same reason
That people could exchange goods
That skills mattered
That a local source needs study

topics.label: Reading Routes Carefully
topics.definition: Information that supports or questions an idea.
facts: Maps of past trade are explanations based on evidence. They are not photographs of every ship journey.
Researchers use objects, written accounts and other sources together. Each source has limits.
Modern country names can help us locate places today, but past borders and communities were different.
quiz: A class draws one solid line for a route they cannot confirm. What would improve the map?
Mark it as uncertain and explain the evidence
Label it certain because it looks neat
Remove every source note
Add imagined journeys as facts
retry: A modern map names China and the Philippines. How should it help a history lesson?
Locate places while remembering past borders differed
Prove modern countries existed in the same form then
Replace all historical sources
Show that every old route is certain
practice: What makes a historical route map stronger?
Clear sources and notes about uncertainty
hard: A written account and an object suggest different details. What should researchers do?
Compare the sources and explain what remains uncertain
Choose the prettier source
Hide the disagreement
Invent a third source

topics.label: Contact Without Sameness
topics.definition: A meeting or connection between people.
facts: Trade brought people into contact. They could share knowledge, ideas and customs as well as goods.
Contact did not make every group alike. Communities could choose, adapt or keep different practices.
The spread of an idea usually needs evidence from more than one object or encounter.
quiz: Two communities trade but keep different customs. What does this show?
Contact can happen without making communities identical
Trade requires everyone to follow one custom
Different customs prove no contact occurred
Exchange can carry goods but never ideas
retry: A visitor teaches a useful skill that people adapt. Which idea fits?
People can adapt knowledge to local needs
Learning always means copying everything exactly
Only goods can move between places
Local people cannot make choices
practice: What can people share through contact?
hard: A class sees a foreign-style object and claims everyone changed religion. What is missing?
Evidence about belief and change, not just one object
A brighter photograph
The object owner's favorite color
A guess presented as fact

topics.label: Useful and Valued Goods
topics.definition: Objects that people make, use or exchange.
facts: Goods could meet different needs. Pots could hold things, while cloth could have everyday and social uses.
The same object may have different uses in different settings. Look for clues rather than guess.
Local goods and imported goods could both be valued.
quiz: A jar is found with clues that it stored food. What is the best explanation?
The jar had a storage use in this setting
Every jar was used only as decoration
Imported goods had no practical uses
One jar proves all people used goods alike
retry: A cloth is used during a gathering. What should you ask before naming its purpose?
How the cloth was used in that community
Which purpose you prefer without evidence
Whether all cloth everywhere had one use
Why local evidence should be ignored
practice: Which is a good people could exchange?
hard: Two similar jars have different find settings. What should a researcher do?
Study each setting before assuming the same use
Give both the same use without checking
Ignore all nearby objects
Assume their shapes reveal every owner

topics.label: Tools Need Knowledge
topics.definition: Ways people use knowledge, skills and tools to do tasks.
facts: Technology includes practical ways of doing things, not just modern machines. Boatbuilding, weaving and pottery use knowledge and tools.
A tool alone does not explain all the skills needed to use it. Learning and practice matter.
People can share techniques and adapt them to materials they have.
quiz: A visitor brings a new tool but nobody knows its use. What else is needed?
Knowledge and practice in using it
Only a new name for it
A rule against asking questions
A claim that tools work by themselves
retry: A maker changes a technique to suit local materials. What does this show?
People can adapt knowledge to their needs
Every technique must be copied exactly
Local materials never matter
Tools remove the need for skill
practice: Which is an example of technology in this lesson?
A skilled way of joining boat planks
hard: A museum displays a weaving tool. Which question would help explain it?
What task did people use it for and what skill was needed?
Was it the favorite color of every maker?
Can its name replace all evidence?
Does it prove everyone wove alike?

topics.label: Ideas Travel Too
topics.definition: Sharing and changing ideas or practices through contact.
facts: People meeting through travel could share language, skills and beliefs. Cultural exchange can move in more than one direction.
A community may change a borrowed idea to suit its needs. Not every group accepts the same ideas.
Sharing is not proof that one society had no ideas of its own.
quiz: Travellers learn a craft and later change it using local materials. What happened?
Knowledge was shared and adapted
The learners lost all their own culture
Only finished goods moved
Every community became the same
retry: Two groups teach each other different skills. What does this show?
Exchange can happen in both directions
Only one group can ever teach
Local knowledge has no value
Every skill began in the same place
practice: Which could travel along with goods?
Only the weight of a basket
A fixed rule that all people must copy
hard: A learner says a borrowed idea was accepted by everyone at once. What should they check?
Evidence of where, when and how people used it
Only whether the story sounds exciting
The color of the map
Whether guesses can replace sources

topics.label: People Make Choices
topics.definition: Change something to suit a need or situation.
facts: Communities were not passive copies of visitors. People made choices about goods and practices.
An adopted design might change as makers used local skills or materials. Some practices continued while others changed.
We need evidence to explain a particular change, not a claim that all change came from outside.
quiz: Local makers add their own design to a technique learned from visitors. Which idea fits?
They adapted the technique
They copied every detail without change
They had no skills before meeting visitors
Their work cannot be part of exchange
retry: A community keeps one tradition while using a new tool. What does this show?
Continuing practices and change can exist together
Every new tool removes all traditions
Traditions never change in any way
New tools prove local people had no choices
practice: Change something to suit a need
hard: A learner explains a new design only by naming foreign visitors. What else matters?
The choices and skills of local makers
Only the visitors' boat color
A rule that local people did nothing
An invented story about every maker

topics.label: A Careful Exchange Report
topics.definition: An idea that can be checked against evidence.
facts: A report should say what its clues support and what they do not show. An object is not a complete record of an encounter.
Combining suitable sources can strengthen an explanation. Missing information should remain visible.
Label imagined scenes as teaching examples, not original historical accounts.
quiz: A bowl shows outside contact, but no record names its trader. What should a report say?
The trader's name is not known from this evidence
Invent a trader's name
Say the bowl lists every stop
Claim every visitor owned it
retry: A classroom story imagines an exchange. How should it be labeled?
A made-up teaching example
An original eyewitness record
Proof of a named ancient trader
A source that needs no checking
hard: A report mixes a real find with an imagined conversation. What is the best improvement?
Separate the evidence from the imagined details
Present both as recorded facts
Remove all source labels
Use the conversation to prove the find's date

title: Early Trading Centers and Maritime Communities

topics.label: Places Where Routes Meet
topics.definition: A place where boats can shelter or stop.
facts: Coasts and river mouths could connect water routes and nearby communities. A suitable stopping place could support exchange.
A location alone does not guarantee a busy trading center. Resources, people and changing conditions also matter.
A harbor scene in this lesson is a teaching model, not a map of one actual port.
quiz: Boats can stop near a river mouth and goods can move inland. Why might this place support trade?
It links water routes and communities
Every river mouth was an identical trading center
Location removes the need for people and goods
Only inland places could exchange products
retry: A sheltered place loses access to a useful route. What should learners consider?
Changing conditions can affect trade connections
A port must stay equally busy forever
Route changes never matter
All trade happens in one fixed place
practice: What is a harbor used for?
hard: Two sites are both near water but have different trade evidence. What should you do?
Compare more than location alone
Call both equally busy without study
Ignore the evidence
Assume one cannot be a real site

topics.label: Butuan: Boats and Goods
topics.definition: A place where people and goods meet for exchange.
facts: Boat remains and imported goods from Butuan help researchers study maritime connections. Different finds can answer different questions.
Boat parts provide clues about construction; traded objects provide clues about contacts. Neither tells every event.
Butuan was one important place, not the only community connected to wider networks.
quiz: At Butuan, researchers study boat parts and imported goods together. Why?
The finds give different clues about maritime connections
Every object tells exactly the same story
The goods identify every boat passenger
Butuan evidence describes every island
retry: A learner says Butuan was the only place that traded. What should you explain?
Important evidence from one place does not rule out other trading communities
A famous site proves no others existed
One boat visited every island
Only large towns could have contact
practice: Which pair helps investigate Butuan's maritime past?
A modern bus ticket and school badge
hard: A new find changes an explanation of a site. What should researchers do?
Review the explanation using the new evidence
Hide the find
Keep every old idea unchanged
Replace evidence with a fictional tale

topics.label: People Behind the Exchange
topics.definition: Something a person does to help an activity.
facts: Maritime communities needed more than visiting merchants. Boatbuilders, food producers and skilled makers could support daily life and exchange.
Different responsibilities could connect people without giving them equal rights or power.
A list of goods alone may not name all the people whose work supported trade.
quiz: A teaching harbor has traders, boat repairers and food producers. What does this show?
Several kinds of work can support maritime life
Only visiting merchants do useful work
All workers necessarily have equal power
Goods move without human work
retry: A report lists imported goods but says nothing about local work. What useful question can you ask?
Whose work helped support the community and exchange?
Why should local people be left out?
Did objects travel by themselves?
Can one list explain every person's life?
practice: People repairing boats and providing supplies
Only people named in one cargo list
hard: A maker contributes goods but has limited choices in society. What should a careful account recognize?
Contribution does not prove equal rights or power
Making goods always means having the most power
A limited choice means no useful work occurred
One worker represents every community

topics.label: Trading Places Change
topics.definition: A difference over time.
facts: Routes and trading places could change over time. Environmental conditions, relationships and needs affected connections.
Evidence from one period cannot automatically describe the same place in every century.
Researchers compare dated finds to explain change rather than assume a place was always the same.
quiz: A site has trade goods from one period but fewer from a later period. What is a careful next step?
Investigate changes and limits in the evidence
Assume the community never existed
Claim the same trade level lasted forever
Invent a single cause without checking
retry: An old map and newer finds show different routes. Which idea helps?
Connections can change over time
All maps show one unchanging route
New evidence should be ignored
Every route always had the same users
practice: What helps study change over time?
Assuming every century was the same
hard: A learner names one reason for a port's decline without sources. What is needed?
Evidence before treating that reason as certain
More confident wording
A longer invented story
A claim that causes never need study

topics.label: Protecting Coastal History
topics.definition: Things and knowledge people value from the past and pass on.
facts: Coastal sites can hold fragile evidence. Moving an object without recording its place can destroy useful information.
Museums, researchers and communities help protect and explain heritage. Visitors should follow site rules.
Caring for a place includes respecting people who live there today, not only studying old objects.
quiz: A visitor finds a possible old pot fragment near a protected site. What should they do?
Leave it and report it to the proper staff
Take it as a souvenir
Wash away everything around it
Sell it before its location is recorded
retry: A class visits a heritage community. Which behavior helps learning?
Follow rules and listen respectfully to local people
Treat residents as part of a display
Enter private places without permission
Collect objects secretly
practice: Why record where an object was found?
Its place can help explain it
It lets anyone own the object
hard: A project protects objects but ignores local concerns. What should improve?
Include respectful dialogue with the community
Keep excluding residents
Assume objects matter but people do not
Publish private details without consent

topics.label: More Than One Way to Communicate
topics.definition: Sharing a message or idea.
facts: People communicated through spoken language, stories, signs and writing. Different forms could serve different purposes.
A written object and an oral account are different kinds of sources. Each needs careful study.
The absence of a surviving written record does not prove that a community had no knowledge or history.
quiz: A learner finds no old written record for a community. What is the careful response?
Look for other sources instead of assuming it had no history
Say its people knew nothing
Invent a written record
Ignore oral traditions and objects
retry: An elder shares a story and a museum shows an inscription. How should learners use them?
Study each kind of source and its limits
Treat them as identical sources
Assume one source answers every question
Reject all spoken knowledge
hard: A class studies a spoken account. What question helps?
Who shared it and what can it help explain?
Why does speech never count as a source?
How can we replace it with a guess?
Does it describe every community?

topics.label: Learning About Baybayin
topics.definition: A set of signs used in writing.
facts: Baybayin is one writing tradition discussed in Philippine history. In its traditional form, many signs represent syllables rather than the same sounds as English letters.
Learning a script needs reliable examples and an understanding of how its signs work. Decorative symbols are not automatically a readable message.
Baybayin should not be used as a name for every script found in the Philippines.
quiz: A learner copies random Baybayin signs and calls them a sentence. What should they do next?
Check the signs and reading rules using a reliable guide
Assume any symbols form a correct sentence
Treat the signs as exactly the English alphabet
Say all Philippine scripts have the same rules
retry: A poster calls every old Philippine script Baybayin. What is a better approach?
Use the correct name and source for each script
Keep one name for all scripts without checking
Ignore the differences
Invent a new name for every object
practice: A set of signs used for writing
hard: A learner wants to write a name in Baybayin. What helps most?
A reliable guide to the script and its sounds
Guessing from shapes alone
Replacing each English letter without checking
Copying a design with no source

topics.label: A Message on Copper
topics.definition: Writing marked on a surface such as metal or stone.
facts: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription bears a date read as 900 CE. Its writing is associated with Kawi, not Baybayin.
It gives evidence of writing and connections with wider Southeast Asian traditions. Specialists study its language and signs.
A single document does not prove that every person could read or that all communities used one script.
quiz: A museum label identifies the Laguna Copperplate writing as Kawi. Which description respects the evidence?
A dated copper inscription with Kawi-related writing
A Baybayin letter written yesterday
Proof that everyone read one script
A complete record of all island communities
retry: A learner says one old written object proves everyone could read. What is missing?
Evidence about who learned and used writing
A brighter display case
The object's modern price
A claim that one object proves everything
hard: A class compares a copper inscription and Baybayin examples. What should it notice?
Different scripts should not be treated as the same
Every old sign is Baybayin
Metal determines the language by itself
All readers used identical writing

topics.label: Writing Traditions Continue
topics.definition: A practice that people continue to use and pass on.
facts: The National Museum presents continuing script traditions among communities including Hanunoo, Buhid, Tagbanua and Pala'wan. These names should not be treated as interchangeable.
Present-day community members are people with choices, not examples frozen in the past.
Learning respectfully means using reliable sources and respecting how communities describe their own knowledge.
quiz: A class labels living script users as people who never change. What should the label say instead?
Their writing traditions continue alongside present-day life
They belong only to the distant past
They all use exactly the same script
They have no say in explaining their traditions
retry: Two communities name their scripts differently. What should learners do?
Use the correct names and learn from reliable community sources
Replace both names with one without checking
Assume the names do not matter
Call every sign a modern invention
practice: People continue using and passing it on
hard: A learner wants to share an example of community writing. What is respectful?
Check its source, meaning and any permission needed
Copy private material without asking
Claim to speak for the whole community
Change its name for convenience

topics.label: Read the Label, Check the Claim
topics.definition: Where information or evidence comes from.
facts: Labels should identify an object or copy, its known context and any uncertainty. A replica is a copy, not the original artifact.
Some old marks are hard to read. Researchers may disagree or be unable to explain all of them.
Honest uncertainty is better than inventing a translation.
quiz: An online image has signs but no source or translation details. What should you do?
Find reliable information before repeating its claims
Assume it is ancient because it looks old
Invent a translation
Call every mark Baybayin
retry: A museum displays a copy of an inscription. Which label is best?
Replica, with information about the original and the copy
Original, even though it is a copy
Proof that all translations are certain
A message written by the visitor
hard: Two readings of an unclear mark differ. What should a report do?
Explain the uncertainty and cite the sources
Hide one reading without reason
Choose the most exciting version as fact
Say all study is useless

topics.label: Choosing Suitable Materials
topics.definition: Something used to make an object.
facts: Makers use knowledge of materials and their properties. A material suitable for one task may not suit another.
Plants, clay, wood and other materials could support many kinds of skilled work. Availability differed by place.
A useful object reflects both materials and human knowledge, not materials alone.
quiz: A maker needs a woven container. Which plan uses knowledge well?
Choose suitable prepared fibers and use weaving skills
Assume any material works without checking
Use a heavy stone as a fiber
Ignore the object's purpose
retry: Two communities use different local materials for similar needs. What does this show?
Knowledge can be applied to different surroundings
Only one community can have skills
Materials never affect making
Both objects must have one origin
practice: Something used to make an object
hard: An object breaks because its material is unsuitable. What should the maker reconsider?
The material's properties and the task
Only its decorative name
Whether skill ever matters
How to avoid every test

topics.label: Learning to Weave
topics.definition: Interlacing strands to make a surface or object.
facts: Weaving can make baskets, mats and textiles. Preparing materials and controlling the pattern require practice.
Weaving traditions differ among communities. Similar-looking objects do not prove identical meanings.
Learning from makers recognizes their skill and their role in passing on knowledge.
quiz: A learner sees a basket and says it was made without planning. Which clue challenges the claim?
Prepared strands arranged in a controlled pattern
Only the color of the display wall
The learner's favorite shape
An unsourced guess
retry: Two woven designs look similar. What should a class avoid?
Assuming they have the same meaning without checking
Looking at how they were made
Reading reliable labels
Asking appropriate questions
hard: A maker explains how fibers must be prepared. What should students recognize?
Material preparation is part of skilled knowledge
Only the finished appearance matters
The object needs no skill
All fibers behave alike

topics.label: Skilled Work Is Technology
topics.definition: Knowledge, methods and tools used to solve tasks.
facts: Technology is not limited to electric devices. Pottery, carving and boatbuilding involve methods and tools.
A maker chooses techniques for a purpose and learns through practice and teaching.
Careful study should not rank a community as less capable because its tools differ from modern ones.
quiz: A student says only electronic objects show technology. Which example corrects the idea?
A skilled method for firing clay containers
Only a phone with a battery
An object appearing without work
A guess with no method
retry: A carving tool differs from a modern machine. What should a learner ask?
How did people use it to do a task?
Why does a different tool prove no skill?
Can modern price explain every use?
Should all old tools be dismissed?
practice: Which activity uses a craft technique?
Shaping and firing a suitable clay pot
hard: A display praises a finished object but not its maker's knowledge. What should be added?
The methods and skills used to make it
Only a larger price tag
A claim that it made itself
An invented story about every maker

topics.label: Designs Need Context
topics.definition: Information about where, when and how something is used.
facts: Designs can have meanings connected with community practices. Not every pattern has the same meaning or is free to copy.
A responsible learner checks how a design is described and whether its use has restrictions.
A classroom activity can explore general making skills without copying sacred or restricted designs.
quiz: A learner wants to copy a design linked with a ceremony. What should happen first?
Check its meaning and whether permission or limits apply
Copy it because it is attractive
Assume all designs belong to everyone
Invent a meaning
retry: A class has no permission to copy a restricted design. What can it do?
Use a teacher-made neutral pattern to study the general skill
Ignore the restriction
Publish the design secretly
Say respect stops all learning
practice: How an object or design relates to its setting
hard: A shop gives a design a made-up community meaning. What should a careful account do?
Check reliable sources rather than repeat the invented meaning
Treat the advertisement as proof
Assume all communities agree
Replace the source with a decoration

topics.label: Keeping Skills Alive
topics.definition: Passing knowledge or skills to others.
facts: Craft knowledge can be passed through teaching, observation and practice. Makers may also adapt to new materials and needs.
Living traditions can continue and change. They are not less meaningful simply because people innovate.
Supporting makers includes crediting them and respecting their choices about sharing knowledge.
quiz: A young maker learns from an elder and tries a new tool. What can this show?
A tradition can continue while some methods change
Any new tool erases all tradition
Only old objects have value
Learning from elders prevents choices
retry: A project uses a maker's explanation without naming its source. What should improve?
Credit the maker and respect agreed sharing limits
Remove the maker from the story
Claim the students invented the skill
Share restricted details without checking
practice: What helps pass on a craft skill?
hard: A maker chooses not to share part of a practice publicly. What is respectful?
Accept the limit and learn from what may be shared
Demand every detail
Record secretly
Assume no permission is needed

topics.label: Many Communities, Many Ways
topics.definition: The presence of differences among people or things.
facts: Philippine communities have different languages, knowledge and practices. Region is one clue, not a complete description of every person.
No single costume, house or custom represents everyone across the islands. Differences also exist within regions.
Comparing communities should help us understand them, not rank their worth.
quiz: A poster uses one costume to represent every Philippine community. What should improve?
Show and explain differences using reliable examples
Say everyone dressed alike
Remove all community names
Rank groups by how unusual they look
retry: Two communities in one region have different practices. What does this show?
Differences can exist within a region
One community must not belong there
Regions always have one unchanging custom
Only faraway places can differ
hard: A learner calls a community less important because its practices differ. What is a better response?
Study differences respectfully without ranking human worth
Agree that difference means less value
Ignore the people's own accounts
Replace their name with a stereotype

topics.label: Surroundings and Human Choices
topics.definition: The surroundings in which people live.
facts: Surroundings can influence available materials and activities. People also make choices and learn from others.
A coastal location does not mean everyone has the same livelihood or belief. Environment alone cannot explain a whole culture.
Understanding a practice needs local evidence and the people's knowledge.
quiz: A coastal village has fishing, weaving and other work. Which idea fits?
Surroundings influence opportunities but do not give everyone one job
Everyone near the sea only fishes
Location decides every belief
Skills do not matter
retry: Two communities use the same plant in different ways. What should learners consider?
Local knowledge, purposes and choices
Only the plant's presence
A rule that their customs must match
A claim that one use cannot be real
practice: Which is part of a community's environment?
hard: A report explains a whole culture using only climate. What is missing?
People's choices, histories and other evidence
Only a brighter map
A rule that people never adapt
More guesses about everyone

topics.label: Listen to Shared Knowledge
topics.definition: Knowledge or stories passed on through spoken forms.
facts: Stories, songs and spoken accounts can carry knowledge and memories. Communities may have rules about who can share some material.
A tradition should be identified and understood in its own setting. A fictional classroom story is not automatically an authentic community tradition.
Respectful study asks about source, meaning and limits.
quiz: A class writes its own story and labels it an ancient community tale. What should change?
Label it a made-up classroom story
Keep the claim because the story is interesting
Name a community without evidence
Say every story has the same origin
retry: An elder shares an account with a limit on public recording. What should students do?
Respect the limit and ask what may be shared
Record secretly
Publish it under their own names
Assume oral material needs no permission
practice: A story passed on through spoken telling
hard: Two versions of an account differ. What is a careful next step?
Ask about sources and settings before explaining the differences
Declare one false without study
Merge both and call every detail certain
Hide all source information

topics.label: Traditions Continue and Change
topics.definition: Something continuing over time.
facts: Traditions can keep important features while changing in some ways. New tools or settings do not automatically end a tradition.
People in living communities decide how to respond to changing needs. No community is frozen in the past.
Compare evidence from different times before claiming either complete sameness or complete change.
quiz: A community keeps a weaving skill while using a newer tool. What might this show?
Continuity and change can happen together
All tradition has disappeared
Nothing can ever change
New tools prove old knowledge was worthless
retry: Two photos from different years show a celebration changed location but kept key practices. What should a report say?
Identify both what continued and what changed
Say every detail stayed the same
Say every tradition ended
Ignore the photo dates
hard: A learner says a living community belongs only in the past. What should improve?
Recognize its present-day life and choices
Treat people as museum objects
Ignore their voices
Assume change removes identity

topics.label: Compare Without Stereotypes
topics.definition: An oversimplified claim applied to every person in a group.
facts: A stereotype treats a group as if every member is the same. It can hide real differences and cause harm.
A careful comparison names its examples, uses evidence and avoids claims about everyone.
Listening to people and checking sources are more helpful than guessing from appearance.
quiz: A learner meets one person and describes everyone in that community the same way. What is the problem?
One person cannot represent every member's experience
Meeting one person proves everything
All groups have one shared personality
Appearance answers every question
retry: A display compares two practices with clear sources and limits. Why is this helpful?
It explains differences without claiming everyone is alike
It ranks one group as worth more
It removes the need to learn from people
It proves no change ever happens
practice: What makes a claim a stereotype?
Applying an oversimplified idea to everyone in a group
Giving a source and a clear limit
hard: A caption makes fun of an unfamiliar practice. What should be done?
Replace mockery with an accurate respectful explanation
Make the joke stronger
Hide the people's own explanation
Assume unfamiliar means wrong

title: Contributions of Early Societies to Filipino Identity

topics.label: Many Contributions to Remember
topics.definition: Something that helps shape a larger whole.
facts: Early societies developed knowledge, skills and ways of living that form part of Philippine heritage. Examples include boatbuilding, making goods and exchanging ideas.
No single community or object explains the whole history of Filipino identity. Many people and later changes also matter.
Recognizing a contribution does not mean claiming every practice stayed unchanged.
quiz: A class chooses only one object to explain all Filipino identity. What would improve the display?
Include different contributions and explain the limits of each example
Say one object tells the whole story
Leave out communities that differ
Pretend later changes never happened
retry: A boatbuilding tradition is part of a heritage lesson. What can it help explain?
One contribution to a wider history of knowledge and skills
Every belief held by every Filipino
The exact life of every sailor
A history with no change
practice: Which is an example of a contribution in this chapter?
A claim that only one group matters
hard: A report praises old skills but says modern identity has no other influences. What is missing?
Other communities and changes over time
Only a more dramatic title
A claim that history stopped
A reason to ignore later evidence

topics.label: Shared Identity, Different Experiences
topics.definition: How people understand and describe who they are.
facts: People may share a Filipino identity while belonging to different communities and traditions. Shared identity does not require sameness in every practice.
The people of the precolonial islands did not all use a single modern national identity in the way we do today.
We can value their contributions without treating the past as identical to the present.
quiz: Two classmates share Filipino identity but have different family traditions. What does this show?
Shared identity can include different experiences
They must keep exactly the same custom
Only one tradition can belong
Differences make shared identity impossible
retry: A learner gives every precolonial person the same modern national identity. What reminder helps?
Ideas of identity and political belonging changed over time
People always used today's identities in the same way
All communities formed one modern nation then
Dates and changes do not matter
practice: How people understand and describe who they are
A rule that everyone must be alike
hard: A display includes only one community's voice. What could make it more balanced?
Include other relevant voices without erasing differences
Call that voice the only possible identity
Remove all community names
Replace sources with a stereotype

topics.label: Show Why an Example Matters
topics.definition: An explanation based on evidence.
facts: A heritage claim needs a reason and evidence. An object may show skill or contact, but it cannot answer every question.
An explanation should connect the evidence with the idea being discussed. Admiration alone is not proof.
When evidence is limited, say so clearly rather than invent details.
quiz: A display says a woven object shows skilled work. Which support is most useful?
Evidence about materials, preparation and weaving methods
Only the maker's imagined favorite color
A claim that praise proves every detail
A price with no source
retry: A jar is used to claim every community had the same beliefs. What should a learner ask?
What evidence connects this object to that broad claim?
Is the jar attractive enough?
Could a longer story make it certain?
Should all questions be avoided?
practice: What is an interpretation in history?
hard: Two explanations fit some clues. What is a careful response?
Compare their evidence and acknowledge uncertainty
Choose by decoration alone
Hide the unanswered questions
Invent proof for a favorite idea

topics.label: Caring Is Part of Learning
topics.definition: Help protect something from loss or harm.
facts: Heritage care includes protecting objects, places and knowledge. Communities have important roles in deciding how their traditions are shared.
Useful actions include following site rules, crediting sources and asking permission when needed.
Respect does not mean taking objects home or publishing everything that can be recorded.
quiz: A student wants a souvenir from a heritage site. Which choice helps protect it?
Leave objects in place and follow site rules
Remove the smallest object
Write on the display
Buy an object taken from the site
retry: A community shares an explanation but not permission to publish a private ritual. What should a class do?
Use only what may be shared and respect the limit
Publish everything because it was seen
Hide the community's name to avoid asking
Treat all knowledge as free to copy
practice: Help protect from loss or harm
hard: A project includes a craftsperson's work. Which step is responsible?
Give credit and check agreed sharing conditions
Claim the students created it
Ignore the maker's wishes
Sell the design without discussion

topics.label: Build a Careful Heritage Story
topics.definition: An idea reached after thinking about evidence.
facts: A strong heritage story connects examples instead of listing objects alone. It explains what each example shows and its limits.
Writing, crafts, maritime links and community traditions reveal different parts of the past. They should not be forced into one identical story.
A respectful conclusion recognizes contributions, diversity and continuing change.
quiz: A class combines writing, boats and weaving in one display. What makes its explanation stronger?
Explain each contribution with sources and note differences
Say all objects prove exactly the same thing
Treat every community as identical
Leave out all source information
retry: A learner finishes with the claim that all traditions remained unchanged. What should be revised?
Recognize both continuing practices and change
Remove every example of change
Call all new practices false
Treat present communities as frozen in time
practice: What should a careful conclusion use?
hard: A final project has attractive images but no explanations. What is the best next step?
Connect the images to supported ideas and name the sources
Add more images without checking
Invent dates to fill space
Assume decoration is the same as learning
